job.style: a diary entry or letter by a student

response.passage: Dear Diary, today in biology class, I learned that cells are the building blocks of life, but they are not all the same. My friend Rohan thought that an elephant must have giant cells compared to a mouse, but our teacher explained that organisms grow by increasing their number of cells, not by making individual cells larger. We also looked at onion peel cells under a microscope. I was surprised to see that even though plants need sunlight for photosynthesis, their root cells do not contain chloroplasts because they live underground. I used to think the nucleus was like a tiny brain that makes decisions, but the teacher clarified that it is actually a storage unit for genetic information, which acts as a blueprint for cell function. We also discussed bacteria, which are prokaryotic. Even though they lack a defined nucleus, they still possess DNA floating in their cytoplasm to carry out life processes. Finally, we learned that the cell membrane is not a solid, sealed wall; it is a selective, porous boundary that allows essential materials to move in and out. It is amazing how these tiny structures work together to keep us alive, whether we are a single-celled organism or a complex human being.
response.summary: Cells are the fundamental units of life that vary in structure based on their function and location. Organisms grow by increasing cell numbers, and cells use DNA and selective membranes to maintain life processes.
